title: Orator
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi040.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: has rerum formas appellat ἰδέας ille non intellegendi solum sed etiam dicendi gravissimus auctor et magister Plato, easque gigni negat et ait semper esse ac ratione et intellegentia contineri; cetera nasci occidere fluere labi nec diutius esse uno et eodem statu. Quicquid est igitur de quo ratione et via disputetur, id est ad ultimam sui generis formam speciemque redigendum.
passages.english: These forms of things Plato, that weightiest authority and teacher not only of thinking but also of speaking, calls *ideai* [ideas], and he denies that they come into being, and says that they exist always and are contained in reason and intelligence; everything else is born, perishes, flows, slips away, and does not remain any longer in one and the same state. Whatever, then, is discussed by reason and method must be brought back to the ultimate form and type of its class.

passages.original: si quidem etiam in Phaedro Platonis hoc Periclem praestitisse ceteris dicit oratoribus Socrates, quod is Anaxagorae physici fuerit auditor; a quo censet eum, cum alia praeclara quaedam et magnifica didicisse tum uberem et fecundum fuisse gnarumque, quod est eloquentiae maximum, quibus orationis modis quaeque animorum partes pellerentur;
passages.english: For indeed in Plato's Phaedrus Socrates also says that Pericles surpassed the other orators in this, that he had been a pupil of Anaxagoras the natural philosopher; from him, he thinks, Pericles not only learned certain other splendid and magnificent things, but also became copious and fertile and knowledgeable (which is the greatest thing in eloquence) about the modes of speech by which each part of the mind is moved;

passages.original: Ac tamen in hoc ipso diligenter examinante verborum omnium pondera reprehendit Aeschines quaedam et exagitat inludensque dura odiosa intolerabilia esse dicit; quin etiam quaerit ab ipso, cum quidem eum beluam appellat, utrum illa verba an portenta sint; ut Aeschini ne Demosthenes quidem videatur Attice dicere.
passages.english: And yet even in this very man, who weighs carefully the force of all his words, Aeschines finds fault with certain things and harasses them, and mockingly says that they are harsh, offensive, intolerable; indeed he even asks him, while calling him a beast, whether those are words or monstrosities; so that to Aeschines not even Demosthenes seems to speak in the Attic manner.

passages.original: facile est enim verbum aliquod ardens, ut ita dicam, notare idque restinctis iam animorum incendiis inridere. Itaque se purgans iocatur Demosthenes: negat in eo positas esse fortunas Graeciae, hocine an illo verbo usus sit, hucine an illuc manum porrexerit. Quonam igitur modo audiretur Mysus aut Phryx Athenis, cum etiam Demosthenes exagitetur ut putidus?
passages.english: For it is easy to pick out some word that is, so to speak, blazing, and to ridicule it once the fires of passion have been put out. And so Demosthenes, clearing himself, jokes: he says that the fortunes of Greece did not depend on whether he used this word or that, or stretched out his hand this way or that. How then would a Mysian or a Phrygian be listened to at Athens, when even Demosthenes is attacked as affected?

passages.original: ecce autem aliqui se Thucydidios esse profitentur: novum quoddam imperitorum et inauditum genus. Nam qui Lysiam sequuntur, causidicum quendam sequuntur non ilium quidem amplum atque grandem, subtilem et elegantem tamen et qui in forensibus causis possit praeclare consistere. Thucydides autem res gestas et bella narrat et proelia, graviter sane et probe, sed nihil ab eo transferri potest ad forensem usum et publicum. Ipsae illae contiones ita multas habent obscuras abditasque sententias vix ut intellegantur; quod est in oratione civili vitium vel maximum.
passages.english: But look, some people declare that they are Thucydideans: a new and unheard-of kind of ignorant men. For those who follow Lysias follow a pleader, not indeed an ample and grand one, but nevertheless subtle and elegant, and one who could hold his ground splendidly in cases in the courts. Thucydides, on the other hand, narrates events and wars and battles, with dignity indeed and properly, but nothing can be carried over from him to forensic and public use. Those very speeches of his contain so many obscure and hidden thoughts that they can scarcely be understood; which is perhaps the greatest fault in political oratory.

passages.original: sed in omni re difficillimum est formam, qui χαρακτὴρ Graece dicitur, exponere optimi, quod aliud aliis videtur optimum. Ennio delector, ait quispiam, quod non discedit a communi more verborum; Pacuvio, inquit alius: omnes apud hunc ornati elaboratique sunt versus, multo apud alterum neglegentius; fac alium Accio; varia enim sunt iudicia, ut in Graecis, nec facilis explicatio quae forma maxime excellat.
passages.english: But in every matter it is most difficult to set out the form of the best, which in Greek is called *charaktēr* [character, type], because one thing seems best to some, another to others. "I delight in Ennius," says someone, "because he does not depart from the common usage of words." "In Pacuvius," says another: "in him all the lines are ornate and carefully worked; in the other there is much more carelessness." Suppose another [prefers] Accius; for judgements vary, as among the Greeks, and it is not easy to explain which form most excels.

passages.original: haec tractasse Thrasymachum Calchedonium primum et Leontinum ferunt Gorgiam, Theodorum inde Byzantium multosque alios, quos λογοδαιδάλους appellat in Phaedro Socrates; quorum satis arguta multa, sed ut modo primumque nascentia minuta et versiculorum similia quaedam nimiumque depicta. Quo magis sunt Herodotus Thucydidesque mirabiles; quorum aetas cum in eorum tempora quos nominavi incidisset, longissime tamen ipsi a talibus deliciis vel potius ineptiis afuerunt. Alter enim sine ullis salebris quasi sedatus amnis fluit, alter incitatior fertur et de bellicis rebus canit etiam quodam modo bellicum; primisque ab his, ut ait Theophrastus, historia commota est, ut auderet uberius quam superiores et ornatius dicere.
passages.english: They say that Thrasymachus of Calchedon and Gorgias of Leontini were the first to treat these things, and then Theodorus of Byzantium and many others, whom Socrates in the Phaedrus calls *logodaidaloi* [word-artificers]; much of their work is clever enough, but, as if only just and for the first time coming into being, it is petty and in some ways like little verses, and too highly coloured. All the more admirable, then, are Herodotus and Thucydides: although their lifetime fell within the period of those I have named, they themselves kept very far from such delicacies, or rather follies. For the one flows without any roughness like a calm river; the other is carried along more vigorously and, speaking of warlike matters, even in a way sounds the call to war; and it was by these first, as Theophrastus says, that history was stirred to venture to speak more copiously and more ornately than [its] predecessors.

passages.original: itaque ut ego, cum a nostro Catone laudabar, vel reprehendi me a ceteris facile patiebar, sic Isocrates videtur testimonio Platonis aliorum iudicia debere contemnere. Est enim, ut scis, quasi in extrema pagina Phaedri his ipsis verbis loquens Socrates: Adulescens etiam nunc, o Phaedre, Isocrates est, sed quid de illo augurer libet dicere. Quid tandem? inquit ille. Maiore mihi ingenio videtur esse quam ut cum orationibus Lysiae comparetur, praeterea ad virtutem maior indoles;
passages.english: So, just as I, when I was praised by our Cato, readily allowed myself even to be criticised by everyone else, so Isocrates, it seems, with the testimony of Plato, ought to despise the judgements of others. For, as you know, almost on the last page of the Phaedrus Socrates speaks in these very words: "Isocrates is still young, Phaedrus, but I should like to say what I foresee of him." "What, then?" says the other. "He seems to me to be of greater talent than to be compared with the speeches of Lysias, and besides [to have] a greater natural disposition to virtue;

passages.original: haec de adulescente Socrates auguratur. At ea de seniore scribit Plato et scribit aequalis et quidem exagitator omnium rhetorum hunc miratur unum; me autem qui Isocratem non diligunt una cum Socrate et cum Platone errare patiantur. Dulce igitur orationis genus et solutum et fluens, sententiis argutum, verbis sonans est in illo epidictico genere quod diximus proprium sophistarum, pompae quam pugnae aptius, gymnasiis et palaestrae dicatum, spretum et pulsum foro.
passages.english: This is what Socrates foretells about [Isocrates as] a young man. But Plato writes this about him as an older man, and he writes it as his contemporary, and, though he is the harasser of all rhetoricians, he admires this one alone; as for me, let those who do not love Isocrates allow me to err along with Socrates and with Plato. A sweet style of speech, then, free and flowing, sharp in its thoughts, sonorous in its words, belongs to that epideictic kind which we have said is proper to the sophists, better suited to the parade than to the battle, dedicated to the gymnasia and the wrestling-school, scorned and driven out of the forum.

passages.original: mira est enim quaedam natura vocis, cuius quidem e tribus omnino sonis, inflexo acuto gravi, tanta sit et tam suavis varietas perfecta in cantibus. est autem etiam in dicendo quidam cantus obscurior, non hic e Phrygia et Caria rhetorum epilogus paene canticum, sed ille quem significat Demosthenes et Aeschines, cum alter alteri obicit vocis flexiones; dicit plorare etiam Demosthenes istum quem saepe dicat voce dulci et clara fuisse.
passages.english: For the nature of the voice is something wonderful: from only three tones in all, the circumflex, the acute and the grave, there arises so great and so sweet a variety, perfected in songs. There is, moreover, also in speaking a kind of less obvious singing, not that peroration of the rhetoricians from Phrygia and Caria, which is almost a chant, but the one which Demosthenes and Aeschines indicate when each reproaches the other with modulations of the voice; Demosthenes even says that the man [Aeschines] wept, whom he often says had a sweet and clear voice.
passages.notes: The final clause is obscure and possibly corrupt; the sense given is tentative.

passages.original: quod quamquam transferendo fit, tamen alio modo transtulit cum dixit Ennius arce et urbe orba sum, alio modo, si pro patria arcem dixisset; et horridam Africam terribili tremere tumultu cum dicit pro Afris immutate Africam: hanc ὑπαλλαγήν rhetores, quia quasi summutantur verba pro verbis, μετωνυμίαν grammatici vocant,
passages.english: Although this is done by transferring, yet Ennius transferred in one way when he said "I am bereft of citadel and city," and in another way [he would have] if he had said "citadel" for "fatherland"; and when he says "bristling Africa trembles with a terrible uproar," putting "Africa" for "the Africans" by a change: this the rhetoricians call *hypallagē*, because words are, as it were, substituted for words, [and] the grammarians call it *metōnymia*,

passages.original: multae sunt eius totae orationes subtiles, ut contra Leptinem; multae totae graves, ut quaedam Philippicae; multae variae, ut contra Aeschinem falsae legationis, ut contra eundem pro causa Ctesiphontis. Iam illud medium quotiens vult arripit et a gravissimo discedens eo potissimum delabitur. Clamores tamen tum movet et tum in dicendo plurimum efficit, cum gravitatis locis utitur.
passages.english: Many of his speeches are plain throughout, like the one against Leptines; many are grand throughout, like some of the Philippics; many are varied, like the one against Aeschines on the false embassy, and the one against the same man on behalf of Ctesiphon's case. The middle style, moreover, he seizes whenever he wishes, and when leaving the grandest style he slips down especially into that. Yet he rouses shouts of applause and achieves most in speaking at the moments when he uses passages of grandeur.

passages.original: atque etiam ante hunc Aristoteles principio artis rhetorical dicit illam artem quasi ex altera parte respondere dialecticae, ut hoc videlicet differant inter se quod haec ratio dicendi latior sit, illa loquendi contractior. Volo igitur huic summo omnem quae ad dicendum trahi possit loquendi rationem esse notam;
passages.english: And even before him Aristotle says at the beginning of his *Art of Rhetoric* that this art corresponds, as it were, as the counterpart to dialectic, so that they differ from each other evidently in this, that this method of speaking is broader, that one of discussion more compressed. I want, therefore, this supreme [orator] to know every method of discussion that can be drawn upon for speaking;

passages.original: conlocabuntur igitur verba, aut ut inter se quam aptissime cohaereant extrema cum primis eaque sint quam suavissimis vocibus, aut ut forma ipsa concinnitasque verborum conficiat orbem suum, aut ut comprehensio numerose et apte cadat. Atque illud primum videamus quale sit, quod vel maxime desiderat diligentiam, ut fiat quasi structura quaedam nec tamen fiat operose; nam esset cum infinitus tum puerilis labor; quod apud Lucilium scite exagitat in Albucio Scaevola: quam lepide lexis compostae ut tesserulae omnes arte pavimento atque emblemate vermiculato!
passages.english: Words, then, will be arranged either so that the ends cohere as aptly as possible with the beginnings and these consist of the most pleasing sounds, or so that the very form and symmetry of the words completes its own circuit, or so that the period closes rhythmically and fittingly. And let us first see what that first [requirement] is like, which especially demands care: that there be a kind of structure, and yet that it not be laboured; for that would be a task both endless and childish; which Scaevola in Lucilius cleverly mocks in Albucius: "How charmingly his phrases are put together, all like little tiles, artfully, in a pavement and an inlaid mosaic!"
passages.notes: lexis is Greek λέξεις (phrases) in Lucilius' line.

passages.original: sed Graeci viderint; nobis ne si cupiamus. quidem distrahere voces conceditur. Indicant orationes illae ipsae horridulae Catonis, indicant omnes poetae praeter eos qui, ut versum facerent, saepe hiabant, ut Naevius: vos, qui accolitis Histrum fluvium atque algidam et ibidem: quam numquam vobis Grai atque barbari.at Ennius saepe Scipio invicte, et semel quidem nos: hoc motu radiantis etesiae in vada ponti.
passages.english: But let the Greeks see to it; for us, not even if we wished it, is it permitted to pull sounds apart. Those somewhat rough speeches of Cato themselves show this; all the poets show it, except those who, in order to make a verse, often admitted hiatus, like Naevius: "you who dwell by the river Hister and chill..." and in the same place: "which never to you Greeks and barbarians..." But Ennius [does it] often, "Scipio invicte" [unconquered Scipio], and I too, once indeed: "hoc motu radiantis etesiae in vada ponti" [by this motion of the shining [one], the etesian winds into the shallows of the sea].
passages.notes: The quoted examples illustrate vowel hiatus; Latin given in brackets where the point depends on sound.

passages.original: quid quod sic loqui, nosse, iudicasse vetant, novisse iubent et iudicavisse? quasi vero nesciamus in hoc genere et plenum verbum recte dici et imminutum usitate. Itaque utrumque Terentius: eho tu, cognatum tuom non noras? post idem Stilponem inquam noveras. Sient plenum est, sint imminutum; licet utare utroque. Ergo ibidem: quae quam sint cara post carendo intellegunt,quamque attinendi magni dominatus sient. Nec vero reprehenderim scripsere alii rem et scripserunt esse verius sentio, sed consuetudini auribus indulgenti libenter obsequor. isdem campus habet inquit Ennius; et in templis:eidem probavit; at isdem erat verius, nec tamen eisdem ut opimius.; male sonabat isdem: impetratum est a consuetudine ut peccare suavitatis causa liceret. Et posmeridianas quadrigas quam postmeridianas quadriiugas libentius dixerim et me hercule quam me hercules.
passages.english: What of the fact that they forbid us to say *nosse*, *iudicasse*, and bid us say *novisse* and *iudicavisse*? As if we did not know that in this type both the full word is said correctly and the shortened one in common usage. So Terence [uses] both: "Hey you, did you not know (*noras*) your kinsman?" and later: "Stilpo, I say, you knew (*noveras*)." *Sient* is full, *sint* shortened; you may use either. So in the same place: "how dear these are they understand afterwards by lacking them, and how great a thing it is to hold on to power (*sient*)." Nor indeed would I criticise *scripsere alii rem* [others wrote the matter], and I feel that *scripserunt* is more correct, but I gladly comply with usage that indulges the ears. "Isdem campus habet," says Ennius; and in an inscription in temples: "eidem probavit"; yet *isdem* was more correct, though not *eisdem*, as Opimius [wrote]; *isdem* sounded bad: usage obtained permission to err for the sake of pleasantness. And I would more gladly say *posmeridianas quadrigas* than *postmeridianas quadriiugas* [afternoon four-horse teams], and *mehercule* rather than *mehercules*.
passages.notes: Text of the Ennius/inscription/Opimius sentence is confused in this edition ("isdem ... eidem ... isdem ... eisdem"); the forms and their attributions are uncertain. Forms kept in Latin because the point is morphological.

passages.original: Sed quis omnium doctior, quis acutior, quis in rebus vel inveniendis vel iudicandis acrior Aristotele fuit? quis porro Isocrati est adversatus infensius? is igitur versum in oratione vetat esse, numerum iubet. Eius auditor Theodectes in primis, ut Aristoteles saepe significat, politus scriptor atque artifex hoc idem et sentit et praecipit; Theophrastus vero eisdem de rebus etiam accuratius. Quis ergo istos ferat, qui hos auctores non probent? nisi omnino haec esse ab eis praecepta nesciunt.
passages.english: But who of all men was more learned, who sharper, who keener in either discovering or judging matters than Aristotle? Who, moreover, opposed Isocrates more hostilely? He, then, forbids verse to be in a speech, but requires rhythm. His pupil Theodectes, a particularly polished writer and craftsman, as Aristotle often indicates, both thinks and teaches this same thing; and Theophrastus [treats] the same matters even more carefully. Who then could bear those people who do not approve of these authorities? Unless they are wholly unaware that these precepts were given by them.

passages.original: quod idem facit in trochaeo, qui temporibus et intervallis est par iambo, sed eo vitiosus in oratione, si ponatur extremus, quod verba melius in syllabas longiores cadunt. Atque haec, quae sunt apud Aristotelem, eadem a Theophrasto Theodecteque de paeane dicuntur.
passages.english: He does the same in the case of the trochee, which is equal to the iamb in quantities and intervals, but is faulty in a speech for this reason, if it is placed at the end, that words end better on longer syllables. And these things which are in Aristotle are said likewise about the paean by Theophrastus and Theodectes.
passages.notes: The subject ('he') is Ephorus, from the preceding context.

passages.original: nec ullum genus est dicendi aut melius aut fortius quam binis aut ternis ferire verbis, non numquam singulis, paulo alias pluribus, inter quae variis clausulis interponit se raro numerosa comprehensio; quam perverse fugiens Hegesias, dum ille quoque imitari Lysiam vult alterum paene Demosthenem, saltat incidens particulas. Et is quidem non minus sententiis peccat quam verbis, ut non quaerat quem appellet ineptum qui illum cognoverit. Sed ego illa Crassi et nostra posui, ut qui vellet auribus ipsis quid numerosum etiam in minimis particulis orationis esset iudicaret.
passages.english: Nor is there any kind of speaking either better or more forceful than striking with two or three words, sometimes with single ones, at other times with a few more, among which a rhythmical period, with varied cadences, occasionally inserts itself; Hegesias, perversely avoiding this, while he too wishes to imitate Lysias, almost a second Demosthenes, hops about chopping up little phrases. And he indeed errs no less in his thoughts than in his words, so that anyone who has come to know him need not look for someone to call foolish. But I have set out those examples of Crassus and of my own so that anyone who wished might judge with his own ears what is rhythmical even in the smallest parts of speech.

passages.original: hanc igitur, sive compositionem sive perfectionem sive numerum vocari placet, et adhibere necesse est, si ornate velis dicere, non solum, quod ait Aristoteles et Theophrastus, ne infinite feratur ut flumen oratio, quae non aut spiritu pronuntiantis aut interductu librari, sed numero coacta debet insistere, verum etiam quod multo maiorem habent apta vim quam soluta. Vt enim athletas nec multo secus gladiatores videmus nihil nec vitando facere caute nec petendo vehementer, in quo non motus hic habeat palaestram quandam, ut quicquid in his rebus fiat utiliter ad pugnam idem ad aspectum etiam sit venustum, sic orator nec plagam gravem facit, nisi petitio fuit apta, nec satis tecte declinat impetum, nisi etiam in cedendo quid deceat intellegit.
passages.english: This, then, whether one chooses to call it arrangement or finish or rhythm, must be employed if you wish to speak with ornament, not only for the reason Aristotle and Theophrastus give, that speech should not run on without limit like a river, since it ought to come to a stop not where the speaker's breath or a copyist's punctuation mark halts it, but where it is constrained by rhythm, but also because what is fitted together has much greater force than what is loose. For just as we see that athletes, and gladiators not much differently, do nothing, whether in guarding cautiously or in attacking vigorously, in which this movement does not have a certain training of the wrestling-school, so that whatever is done usefully for the fight in these matters is also graceful to look at, so the orator neither deals a heavy blow unless the thrust was well fitted, nor evades an attack with enough cover unless he understands what is becoming even in giving ground.
passages.notes: 'interductu librari': 'librari' is the genitive of librarius (copyist), referring to a punctuation mark inserted by a scribe. 'nec vitando... nec petendo' after 'nihil' is a double negative used for emphasis; rendered as affirmative sense ('do nothing... in which').
